King and Priest (Distinction of Offices)
KING and PREEST
noun (typology; office)
From king, Old English cyning, ruler; and priest, Greek presbuteros through Latin presbyter; the distinction of crown and altar under the old covenant.

Biblical Definition

Under the old covenant God set a wall between the office of king and the office of priest, that no man might join in himself the crown and the altar — until Christ, of whom both spoke, should unite them in His own person. King Uzziah of Judah, "when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense" (2 Chr 26:16). Fourscore priests withstood him, saying, "It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense" (2 Chr 26:18). The king raged, "and while he was wroth with the priests, the leprosy even rose up in his forehead" (2 Chr 26:19), and he was a leper to his death, cut off from the house of the LORD. The crown was of Judah, the altar of Aaron and Levi; the two were not to be confounded. Yet the prophet foresaw their union: "he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne" (Zech 6:13). This is fulfilled only in Christ, a priest after the order of Melchizedek, who is "King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace" (Heb 7:2). This dictionary confesses that the old-covenant separation of offices guarded the holiness of God and pointed forward to the one Mediator, our King and Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

The old-covenant separation of the kingly and priestly offices, dramatized in Uzziah's leprosy when he usurped the altar. The two offices were kept apart until Christ, priest after Melchizedek, lawfully unites crown and altar in Himself.

KING AND PRIEST, noun. The distinction of the royal and priestly offices under the old covenant.

Dramatized in King Uzziah, struck with leprosy for usurping the priests' work of burning incense.

"It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron" (2 Chr 26:18).

It kept the crown of Judah and the altar of Aaron apart, that the holiness of God be guarded.

It is resolved only in Christ, who "shall be a priest upon his throne" (Zech 6:13; Heb 7).

Key Scripture

2 Chr 26:16 — "But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense."

2 Chr 26:19 — "Then Uzziah was wroth, and had a censer in his hand to burn incense: and while he was wroth with the priests, the leprosy even rose up in his forehead before the priests in the house of the LORD, from beside the incense altar."

Zech 6:13 — "Even he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both."

Heb 7:2 — "To whom also Abraham gave a tenth part of all; first being by interpretation King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace;"

Modern Corruption

The lesson of the distinction is lost wherever men presume to seize an office God has not given them, blurring the lines of authority that Scripture and Christ's order set.

expand to see more

Uzziah's sin was presumption: strong and successful, his heart was lifted up, and he reached for an office that was not his. The standing warning is against any usurpation of God-appointed office — whether the magistrate intruding upon the things of God, or, in the church, those who grasp at an office Christ has not conferred. The Roman papacy provides a grave instance, claiming both temporal and spiritual supremacy in one man, a confounding of crown and altar that Scripture never grants to any but Christ. God guards the boundaries of office, and He humbles those who leap them, as Uzziah was made a leper to his death.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is the glory of Christ, in whom the two offices are at last lawfully one. The old covenant kept king and priest apart precisely to magnify the wonder that the Branch "shall be a priest upon his throne" (Zech 6:13). He alone, a priest after Melchizedek who needs no Aaronic descent, rules and intercedes together; and so the very separation that condemned Uzziah exalts the Lord Jesus, our King and our Priest forever.

Hebrew Roots

The distinction sets the royal line of Judah apart from the priestly line of Aaron, two offices joined only in the antitype, Christ after the order of Melchizedek.

expand to see more

Hebrew melek, king, of the tribe of Judah; the throne was not Levitical.

Hebrew kohen, priest, of the sons of Aaron and the tribe of Levi; the altar was not royal.

Uzziah's name means "the LORD is my strength," the very strength that lifted his heart to ruin.

Melchizedek, "king of righteousness" and "king of Salem," held both offices as a type (Heb 7:1–2).

The Branch of Zechariah 6:13 unites throne and altar, fulfilled in Christ alone.

Usage

"He cited the king-priest distinction to show why no mere man may claim both crown and altar."

"Uzziah's leprosy teaches the king-priest distinction: God humbles those who seize an office not their own."

"Only in Christ is the king-priest distinction lawfully resolved, for He is priest upon His throne."
